The lifetime cost of recurring fees: follow the dollars and the growth

Compare two fee assumptions with a common savings plan, then separate direct deductions from their effect on future investment growth.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Hypothetical identical investments before fees. Annual fees are effective fractions of assets, converted to equivalent monthly charges. Every month: investment growth, then fee on the grown opening balance, then a month-end contribution. Net annual growth factor is (1 + gross return) × (1 − annual fee). The central idea

Recurring fees change both the money deducted and the balance left to compound. Compare costs, services and risk on a consistent basis when assessing a long-term plan.

01

Compare costs against the same saving effort

The charts hold the initial balance, monthly contributions, horizon and gross investment return constant. Only the recurring fee changes between the paths. This isolates the cost mechanism without claiming that two real investment arrangements provide identical investments, risks or services.

The Canadian Securities Administrators’ fee overview identifies several types of charges associated with investment products, accounts, transactions and advice. Understanding the applicable charges helps clarify what the investor pays and what services are received.

The no-fee line is a mathematical reference. It does not identify an available product or promise equivalent services at zero cost. Before comparing actual arrangements, check which costs are included, which are additional and whether the investment exposures and service scope are comparable.

02

State how the percentage becomes a deduction

This model treats the annual fee as an effective fraction of assets and converts it to an equivalent monthly fraction: monthly fee = 1 − (1 − annual fee)1/12. Each month the opening balance first earns the gross return, the fee is deducted from that grown balance, and the contribution then arrives at month-end.

The resulting annual growth factor before contributions is (1 + gross return) × (1 − annual fee). With 5% gross return and a 0.25% fee, the modeled net annual rate is 4.7375%. With a 1.75% fee, it is 3.1625%. Simply subtracting fee from gross return would use a different, approximate convention.

Actual charges may accrue daily, apply to different valuation bases, include tax or use flat-dollar schedules. The tool’s convention is explicit so its results can be checked. If an entered return already includes a particular charge, deducting that same charge again would count it twice.

03

Read the difference in ending wealth

The default example begins with CAD 10,000 and adds CAD 500 each month for 30 years. At the selected 5% gross return, fee A of 0.25% leaves CAD 429,421.33. Fee B of 1.75% leaves CAD 322,759.38. The difference is CAD 106,661.95 under this smooth-return illustration.

That difference is not a bill issued in the final year. It accumulates from deductions over time and the return those deducted amounts would otherwise have experienced. The common contributions remain the same, so the comparison does not disguise an additional saving effort in one case.

Fee A and fee B are editable labels, not a fixed ranking. If B is set below A, the sign of the displayed A-minus-B difference changes. If both fees are equal, the paths and ending values coincide. Neither setting predicts how differently managed real portfolios will perform before costs.

04

Separate direct fees from the return effect

The fee bars total the monthly dollar deductions. They are nominal amounts paid at different dates, added without discounting or inflation adjustment. The waterfall starts with the no-fee reference, subtracts fee B’s direct deductions and reconciles the remaining return effect to fee B’s ending value.

Under positive constant gross returns, money deducted earlier misses later positive growth. Under negative constant gross returns, the removed amounts would instead have experienced losses. The residual return effect can then reverse sign. This accounting effect is not a refund, another fee or evidence that charging a fee improves the investment.

The matrix compares selected recurring fees over different horizons against the matching no-fee reference for each horizon. Darker cells show larger ending-wealth gaps. They are cumulative differences, with no probability attached, rather than annual fee rates expressed as dollars.

05

Bring the cost assumption into the goal review

Use a consistent after-cost return assumption when estimating whether a savings goal is funded. If a cost change reduces the modeled endpoint, quantify the resulting gap before choosing a response. Contributions, timing, spending goals and service arrangements are separate decisions.

For an actual account, inventory recurring product charges, advisory costs, account fees and transaction costs, and identify any overlap. Compare that inventory with the investment and service terms. This calculator includes only the selected recurring percentage; it does not value advice, determine suitability or calculate a household’s tax treatment.

Review fees when the account, product mix or service arrangement changes. A transparent cost assumption makes the long-term plan easier to assess, while leaving investment uncertainty and the value of the services as questions requiring their own evidence.
